title: Three hundred years of the Khalsa
hookLine: crowds gather at Anandpur Sahib to mark three hundred years of the Khalsa
tomorrow: Four hundred years of the Granth

cards: A town in the Shivalik hills, its roads packed with people on foot, on tractors, on the backs of trucks. Saffron and blue everywhere. Langar tents stretch along the roadside, serving anyone who sits down.
Nagar kirtan processions sing their way toward the gurdwara. The place is Anandpur Sahib, and the crowds have come home to the spot where, tradition says, the Khalsa was born on a Vaisakhi morning.
The count has reached a round number. Today: three hundred years of the Khalsa.

teach.b: First, the morning being remembered. In the tradition Macauliffe records, Guru Gobind Singh stood before the gathered Sikhs at Anandpur at Vaisakhi and asked for a head. One by one, five came forward.
They became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, and they received amrit. Then the Guru asked them to give amrit to him: the teacher asked his own students to initiate him.
This path told that story long ago; today it's being remembered. Second, the gathering.
When the count reached three hundred years, Sikhs came back to Anandpur Sahib in crowds, and gurdwaras far from Punjab marked it with kirtan, amrit ceremonies and nagar kirtans in their own streets.
It counts back to a beginning and asks: are we still the people that morning made?
Fourth, this week's answer. Volunteers tore down a rebuilt shrine and raised it again with their own hands. A sangat cleaned a pool by passing basins along a line.
A soft-spoken Sikh led India's government. A Partition orphan became Milkha Singh. A physicist sent light around a bend.
Writers kept the story, in many languages.
That's the panth's long line, still running from that morning: ordinary Sikhs, keeping faith in public, three centuries on.

how: Sikhs mark Vaisakhi each year as the birth of the Khalsa, with kirtan, amrit ceremonies and nagar kirtan processions; round-number anniversaries draw large gatherings at Anandpur Sahib and in gurdwaras worldwide.

games.q: you're one of the five, and you've just received amrit. the Guru now stands before you and asks for it too. what happens?
o: you refuse: a student can't give to the teacher.
you give him amrit, as he asks.

games.why: in the tradition, the Panj Pyare gave amrit to Guru Gobind Singh: the teacher was initiated by his own students.

practice: Bring to mind one beginning in your own life that still matters: a wedding, a birth, a move, a first day, a promise you made.

Go back to that morning, where you were and who was there, and ask the anniversary question gently: am I still the person that morning made? Let the answer be honest, and kind; if you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
